Taken as a whole, this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of the charity of ordinary beings and sages;

taken separately, it originally stems from the Bodhisattva’s initial observance of the two hundred and fifty precepts and his cultivation of fundamental dhyāna and other meditations, wherein he gives rise to compassion within each and every wholesome factor that serves to prevent unwholesome states.
The fundamental vow of compassion permeates the King Samādhi; not abandoning sentient beings, it responds to their specific needs so that each may obtain benefit.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"The twenty-five samādhis shatter the twenty-five realms of existence. This is the second of the ten points, summarized as follows.

Third, regarding the benefit for the śrāvakas: if a person loathes birth-and-death, yet undergoes death through birth and returns to birth through death, exhausting their spirit and wandering in transmigration without end;
obscured by craving and desire like a wild ox that loves its own tail, they fail to attain liberation.
Therefore it is said: if a person encounters suffering and becomes weary of old age, illness, and death, one preaches *nirvāṇa* for them so that they may reach the end of all suffering;
once they have become weary within their hearts and are resolutely determined to seek liberation, for this purpose, they cultivate the path of the *śrāvaka*.
If, while observing the precepts, the rākṣasas of craving and views damage the life-preserving float, the precepts will become impure.
Because the precepts are impure, samādhi will not manifest.

Since there is neither precept nor concentration, the outflow-free state does not arise; therefore, one must single-mindedly cultivate precept, concentration, and wisdom. When there is an opportune condition capable of opening the gateway, the power of the four samādhis—such as the Immaculate and others—is invoked to ensure that karma of the four realms of existence does not arise, thereby purifying the precepts.
If one cultivates both concentration and wisdom equally, then if wisdom possesses concentration, the wisdom will not be deranged;
if concentration possesses wisdom, the concentration will not be deluded. This is called being "worthy" (xian), and the worthy are said to be neighbors to the sages.
Cultivating this concentration and wisdom, one should practice with single-minded diligence as if one’s head were on fire.

Yearning for dhyāna and wisdom like a thirsty person seeking a drink, yet being disturbed by the twenty-one types of tainted karma, one must apply the power of the various samādhis. When concentration gives rise to the clarity of contemplation, the four roots of goodness are perfected; as the path of subduing becomes matured, in a single kṣaṇa one undergoes transformation and immediately realizes the truth, becoming a srotāpanna. One thus destroys the afflictions of the views regarding the twenty-five states of existence and the eighty-eight latent tendencies.

This constitutes the twenty-fifth empowerment of the samādhis, which causes one to sever the delusions of the truths to be seen (satyadarśana-heya) while simultaneously eliminating the four types of volition (cetanā).
Therefore, it is said:
"The sixteenth moment of mind immediately enters the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)"; such is its meaning.

Next, one enters the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If one is a person of superior capacity, they apply the power of thirteen samādhis all at once to shatter the five lower-tier afflictions of the realm of desire (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-kleśa*).

If one is a person of duller capacity, they sever the afflictions of thought (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) stage by stage, applying samādhi accordingly at each stage until the afflictions of the three realms are exhausted; this is the ultimate benefit of the Samādhi of True Reality (*tattva-samādhi*).
Regarding the intermediate benefit of grass within this context:
taken collectively, it arises from the power of the roots of goodness of the benevolence of both ordinary beings and sages;

taken individually, it arises from fundamental compassion. Initially, by contemplating the goodness of analyzing emptiness and extinguishing form within the ten dharma-realms, one gives rise to great vows and perfumes the King Samādhi, thereby not abandoning sentient beings and resulting in the intermediate benefit of grass within existence.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that the twenty-five samādhis destroy the twenty-five states of existence; this is the third of ten sections, and the general meaning is as follows.

Regarding the fourth section, the benefits for pratyekabuddhas: if a person possesses deep and sharp roots of past goodness, they will, in an age without a Buddha, feel weary of birth and death, delight in solitary tranquility, and contemplate profound causes and conditions.
The text states:
"One who has previously made offerings to the Buddhas and aspired to seek the supreme Dharma is taught the path of the Pratyekabuddha.

Such a person possesses great merit and is fit to be inspired; the Sage responds to them by appearing before them, causing flowers to fall and bracelets to tinkle, so that they may obtain both hidden and manifest benefits and awaken to the path of the Pratyekabuddha.
This still pertains to the benefits of the intermediate grasses.
As for the Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage and the six perfections, they contemplate the Four Noble Truths and practice the conduct of the six perfections.

When practicing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), if someone comes to beg for their head, or demands their eyes, their kingdom, city, wife, or children, and their mind wavers or shifts, the perfection of giving is not accomplished; they recognize this within themselves as evil.

If one wishes to accomplish the virtue of giving (*dāna*), one may activate the opportune faculty; by relying on the power of samādhi, one subdues the obscuration of stinginess. This is the destruction of the existence of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Once the obscuring mind has departed, one gives with joy, as if drinking nectar (*amṛta*).

To know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are precarious, fragile, and impermanent is the benefit of the samādhi of delighting the deluded mind; it is the benefit of its hidden and manifest aspects.
If ethical discipline (*śīla*) is perfected, this subdues the obscuration of violating precepts and destroys existence in hell; this is the benefit of the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*).
The perfection of patience subdues the obscuration of anger and destroys the existence of animals; it is the benefit of non-retrogressive samādhi.
The perfection of dhyāna subdues the obscuration of distraction and destroys the existence of humans; it is the benefit of the four samādhis.
Vigor accomplishes the subduing of the obscuration of indolence; it destroys the existence of the asuras and is the benefit of the Samādhi of Joy.
Wisdom accomplishes the subduing of the obscuration of ignorance; it destroys the existence of the devas and is the benefit of the seventeen samādhis.
The six obscurations are the karma of the six realms of existence, as fully set forth in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

Because one subdues the karma of the six realms, one is not afflicted by these obscurations; one attains the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), wanders through the six realms, and accomplishes the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
This is precisely the aforementioned benefit of the grasses.

Generally, it should be understood as before; however, to discuss it specifically: by contemplating the good and evil within the phenomena of the ten dharma-realms, one gives rise to great vows, which permeate the three samādhis, never abandoning sentient beings, and so forth.
Sixth, regarding those who benefit through general access: these are the practitioners common to the Three Vehicles.
Whether they are at the stage of Dry Wisdom, the Stage of Nature, or the Stage of the Eight Persons’ Vision, they are benefited by means of the twenty-five samādhis.
From the stage of Dry Wisdom up to the tenth stage, one employs twenty-one samādhis to further eliminate the afflictions of thought.
Moreover, by gradually eradicating ignorance, this is called the "benefit of the small tree."
The general and specific aspects of compassion may be understood by analogy with what preceded, and so forth.

Regarding the seventh section, the benefit for individuals: this refers to the stage of the sequential mind (*anupūrva-citta*), wherein one binds the object of focus to the *dharmadhātu*. By contemplating the *dharmadhātu* in a single thought-moment, one enters the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) and attains the benefit of the Samādhi of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
by entering the Ten Practices (*daśa-carita*) and the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), one attains the benefit of the Samādhi of Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Upon entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one attains the benefit of the Samādhi of the Middle Truth (*madhyamaka-satya*).
This is precisely the benefit of the great tree.
The general and specific aspects of compassion are to be understood by analogy with what was previously stated, and so forth.
Eighth, regarding the benefit for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jen): this is the practice of the principle of the three truths as one reality.
Within a single thought-moment, the dharma-realm is the object of focus; the dharma-realm is the condition upon which the mind is bound.

When encountering conditions and objects throughout daily life, every lifting and setting down of the feet is the site of enlightenment (dōjō). One’s mind, in every moment of thought, accords with the various *pāramitās*, practicing the four samādhis and contemplating the ten kinds of objects.
When the opportunity for liberation arises, the Sage responds accordingly, causing one to awaken with sudden clarity.
Whether this awakening is partial or complete, one obtains both hidden and manifest benefits.

This is the perfect application of the twenty-five samādhis, wherein the perfect practice breaks through the twenty-five realms of existence to reveal the nature of the self, thereby attaining the benefit of ultimate reality.
The ninth point, regarding the benefit of transformation (pariṇāma), refers to the benefit for those in the land of skillful means with remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*).

Within the preceding eight points, there are four or nine locations—namely, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), the thirty minds of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), and the semblance-understanding of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*)—who merely destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) but have not yet eliminated ignorance (*avidyā*). Moistened by ignorance, their outflow-free merit (*anāsrava-puṇya*) results in birth within this land of skillful means.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:

"I become a Buddha in other lands under different names; when one seeks the wisdom of a Buddha in those realms and hears this sutra, that is precisely what constitutes entry into the One Vehicle in those lands."
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"Three types of beings are born in the land of transformation (nirmāṇa-bhūmi): namely, the Arhats of Great Power, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* speaks of the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*): [as follows:]
First, the body born of the intention for the dharma of peace and bliss; this is intended for those of the Two Vehicles, representing their intention to enter the peace and bliss of nirvana.

Second, the body born of the intention of samādhi; this is intended for those of the Shared Teaching who emerge into the provisional realm to transform sentient beings, employing the intention of supernatural powers and samādhi.
Third, the *svabhāva-manomaya-kāya* (self-nature mind-made body). This corresponds to the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) which cultivates the self-nature of the Middle Way.
Generally speaking, "mind" (*manas*) refers here to the intention to establish peace and bliss as emptiness, and the intention to manifest through samādhi.
The meaning of "mental application" (*manasikāra*) refers to the stage of "cultivating one's own nature.
Whether it be the Separate Teaching or the Perfect Teaching, as long as one has not yet given rise to true realization, all such stages are termed "mental application.
Thus, the Treatise says:
"At this time, having transcended the stage of mind (manobhūmi), one dwells within the activity of wisdom (jñānakarman).
If true realization has been aroused, it is indeed the activity of wisdom; if true realization has not yet been aroused, it still remains within the stage of mind.
Those who take rebirth in that [state] are dull in their analysis of phenomena (dharma),
while those who realize the essence of phenomena are sharp;
those who distinguish individuals have already practiced the conventional (prajñapti) and are thus somewhat sharper still.
The person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) is already identical with the Middle Way and is thus the most sharp.
Since there is this distinction between the sharp and the dull, their cultivation and study therein involve two types of benefit: gradual and non-gradual.
Furthermore, this involves both sequential and non-sequential application through the twenty-five samādhis.

This constitutes the skillful means for nine types of persons to be born in the Land of Expedient Means; beginning from that land, they perceive the existence of a self-nature and thereby attain the most ultimate benefit.
If distinguished according to their conceptual analysis, it is said that the land of skillful means lies outside the triple world;
yet if one considers the reality of things as they are, it need not be far away.
As the subsequent text states:

"If one can believe and understand with a profound mind, then one will see the Buddha always dwelling on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma."
This refers to the benefit of the *upāya-bhūmi* (the land of skillful means).
Regarding the tenth section, "the benefit of the *samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi* (the land of true retribution)," this refers to the benefit for those in the *samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi*.

Within the eighth section, there are two people who are born into the *upāya-bhūmi*; furthermore, it is only those two who have completely shattered ignorance (*avidyā*) and perceived the true reality (*dharmatā*) that are able to be born there.

However, the instances of ignorance are exceedingly numerous; thus, although the Three Sages and Ten Sages dwell in the stage of true retribution, as long as that retribution is not yet exhausted, residual delusions remain, which are further remedied by the forty-one applications of the King Samādhi.
As for the state of wondrous enlightenment, it vertically exhausts the past and horizontally pervades all things, being neither born nor extinguished;
because it is neither born nor extinguished, ignorance is forever exhausted and wisdom is perfectly fulfilled, and thus it is said to be "neither born nor extinguished."
Furthermore, because the conditions for response are fulfilled and the benefit is ultimate, it is said that there is neither birth nor extinction.
If one speaks in terms of analytical distinction, it is said that the true recompense lies beyond the stage of skillful means;
yet if one takes phenomena as they are and realizes their reality, this is not far removed from it.
The text says:

"One perceives that in this Sahā world, the ground is made of lapis lazuli, level and even; its various terraces and towers are composed of all kinds of jewels, and pure bodhisattvas alone dwell therein."
This refers precisely to the meaning of the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*).

Whether it concerns coarse or subtle capacities, the responses of the Separate or Perfect [Vehicles], pure or impure lands, or shallow or deep benefits, none fall outside these ten sections. They encompass the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and their benefit is roughly complete; thus the general intent is evident and need not be elaborated with further prolixity.
Thus, at the abode of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, the poisonous drum harms living beings; though the hearing of its sound may be distant or near, death may be either prolonged or sudden.
The celestial drum increases the Path; though the hearing of its sound may be distant or near, [the result] is likewise.

Therefore, there arise further distinctions of depth and shallowness, leading to the attainment of benefits through both karma and vows, which correspond to the various retinues and their respective interests.
Question:

Since the first section has already refuted the twenty-five states of existence and brought the attainment of benefit to completion, there would be nothing further to refute and no further benefit to discuss; why then is it necessary to proceed to ten sections?
Answer:
First, one destroys the twenty-five kinds of suffering that are karmic retribution and obtains the benefit of the fruit of retribution.
Next, one destroys the twenty-five kinds of suffering that are causes and obtains the benefit of cultivating the cause.
Next, one breaks through the views of the twenty-five states of existence and the suffering of afflictions (kleśa), thereby attaining the benefit of true samādhi.

Next, one breaks through the twenty-five kinds of emptiness, causing one to emerge from the provisional nature of the twenty-five states of existence, thereby attaining the benefit of conventional samādhi.
Next, by destroying the two extremes of existence and emptiness regarding the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), one manifests the benefit of the sovereign samādhi of the Middle Way.
Next, by destroying the land of expedient means with remainder and emerging from the twenty-five provisional designations, one attains the benefits of both the conventional and sovereign samādhis.
Next, the refutation of the real reward land serves only to profoundly manifest the benefits of the King Samādhi.
For those who have not yet fully realized the three truths, the intent of the benefit does not cease; thus, there are ten sections, the meaning of which is as follows.
Question:
Do the three truths exist exclusively in the ultimate stage, or can they also extend to ordinary beings?
Answer:
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Sentient beings consist of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It further states:
“Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are peerless.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:
“The nature of phenomena is form; the nature of phenomena is feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.”
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Thus, from the ordinary person to the sage, all are existent; this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"The suchness of sentient beings, the suchness of Maitreya, and the suchness of the worthy and noble ones are one suchness, not two suchnesses."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Form is empty; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.
If there were even a single dharma that transcended nirvāṇa, it too would be like an illusion and like a magical transformation."
This means that both the ordinary person and the sage are empty; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"In the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), is there a self or not?"
He replied:
"There is a self; this self is the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is the Middle Way.
Among all phenomena produced by causes and conditions, not a single form or a single fragrance is not the Middle Way."
Thus, from the ordinary person to the sage, all are entirely within the Middle Way, the primary truth of ultimate meaning.
Question:
To discuss the benefits at such length, the scriptural passages seem excessive.
The first says:
"Since time immemorial, I have praised and shown the path to nirvana; that the suffering of birth and death is forever ended—I have always spoken thus.
The second says:
"In the past, at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas, I taught them the unsurpassed path.
The third [chapter] says:
"I shall now speak of the causal conditions from my former lives."
"On what textual authority is this based?
Answer:
The first text states directly:
Regarding the phrase "from kalpas long ago," the expression "long ago" is indeed profound and vast, yet it does not explicitly reveal the original ground; perhaps it refers to an intermediate period.
The second passage states directly:

"In the past, [he was at] the places of twenty-two trillion Buddhas. Since the number of kalpas is not specified, the duration—whether long or short—is difficult to clarify; however, judging by the subsequent text, it appears to be relatively recent.

Now, to discuss the benefit of the distant future, we take the third passage: "If one were to take ink from a trichiliocosm and, passing eastward beyond a thousand worlds, drop a single dot, and if every dot and non-dot were ground into dust, with each speck of dust representing one kalpa, and then further passing through immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
"By this clear testimony, looking back to the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, that time was but yesterday.

From that point onward, it has served as the beginning of the Mahāyāna; those Buddhas preached the sutras for eight thousand kalpas, and the sixteen princes expounded them again for eighty-four thousand kalpas."

The sutras and śāstras of that [Buddha] are extensive in text and profound in meaning; at that time, among the audience, some may attain realization on the very seat, some may be transformed midway through, and some may be transformed upon arriving later—all shall reach the Precious Place, receive the Dharma-nature body, and become their kinsmen of rebirth.
Secret within and manifest without, they bring sentient beings to maturity together and perform the work of a Buddha.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Though he has attained the Way and turned the wheel of Dharma, he continues to practice the bodhisattva path."
This is the intended meaning.
At that time, the audience has not yet attained the benefit of ultimate reality; as for the benefit of its semblance, it is not forgotten across lifetimes.
As for the benefits of the practice of contemplation through names, they are forgotten across lifetimes, though there may be some who do not forget them.
Regarding "forgetting": if one encounters a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), the latent roots of past goodness will arise again;
if one encounters an evil companion, one loses the original mind. Therefore, there are various kinds of treatments and cauterizations during this intermediate period.
Some are matured through the Mahāyāna, while others are matured through the Hīnayāna.

Those who employ skillful means, though they may teach various paths, in reality do so for the sake of the One Vehicle; furthermore, they cause all beings to reach the place of treasure and receive the Dharma-nature body.
Furthermore, in that land, they receive the ninth and tenth levels of true benefit;
the Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand worlds are precisely those who belong to this stream.
These matters have already been fully concluded above and are termed "benefits over a long period.
As for those among the sentient beings therein who currently abide on the stage of the Śrāvaka, their more immediate benefits will be discussed further below, as stated at length.
